Lumio — Behind the Dashboard: the Machine-Learning Pipeline, Step by Step¶

Load → Clean → EDA → Feature engineering → Train/test split → Train → Evaluate → Tune → Score live data → Monitor¶

The live dashboard shows results: alerts, expected-vs-actual charts, the heatmap. This notebook opens the back end and runs every step that produces those results, by hand, one cell at a time.

This is not a copy of the back end. The notebook imports Lumio's own production modules (lumio.ingest, lumio.quality, lumio.model, lumio.db) and points them at a private notebook database, so what you see here is exactly what the app does.

Step Pipeline stage What you will see Back-end code used
0 How live data flows Does Lumio update with every transaction? (explanation + diagram)
1 Data load One transaction → 5-minute summary; load from CSV and from SQL; streaming ingestion world, db, ingest
2 Cleaning Validation, the data-quality gate (hold / dedup), aggregation quality.check, model.aggregate
3 EDA for modelling Targets, transformations, what drives them —
4 Feature engineering The 9 features Lumio uses and the ones it deliberately does not use model.features, world.is_payday
5 Train / validation / test split Time-based split, and why a random split cheats —
6 Model training & evaluation Seasonal baseline vs linear regression vs gradient boosting; MAE, RMSE, R², MAPE same settings as model.Baseline
7 Hyperparameter tuning Randomised search with time-series cross-validation; validation curve —
8 From prediction to anomaly score Noise model, robust per-segment spread, z-scores; proof the notebook = the app model.Baseline
9 Threshold tuning & detection metrics Precision / recall / F1 vs sensitivity; confirmation scans; incidents caught same rules as detector
10 Live scoring: what the dashboard shows Stream batches into the database, score them, rebuild the dashboard chart and heatmap from SQL ingest.store, bucket_scores table
11 Monitoring & retraining Daily accuracy, drift, saving and loading the model Baseline.save / load
12 Summary & professor's questions Pipeline map + likely viva questions —

Run: from the analysis folder, pip install -r requirements.txt then Run All (about 2 minutes). It creates its own pipeline_demo.db; it never touches the live app's database.

0. How live data flows — does Lumio update with every transaction?¶

Short answer: every payment is counted, but not every payment triggers a calculation. Lumio works the way real monitoring works at a bank:

Layer Happens What it does
Each payment Continuously (≈ 2 million a day in this network) The bank's monitoring collector counts it: success or failure, how long it took, its amount, segment and app version
5-minute summary Every 5 minutes The collector sends one row per segment (48 rows): volume, successes, p95 time, average amount, plus a small sample of individual transactions for investigations
Ingest → database Every 5 minutes ingest.store() validates the batch and writes it to the metrics table
Scoring Every 5 minutes Each new row is compared with what the model expects for that segment at that moment → the live chart (bucket_scores)
Scan Every 15 minutes Quality gate → z-scores → grouping → 2-scan confirmation → alert, routing, email (window_scores, incidents, outbox)
Model training Once on 3 weeks of history (in production: re-trained on a schedule, e.g. monthly) Learns what normal looks like for every segment, hour, weekday and payday

So the data updates every 5 minutes, but the model does not change with each transaction, and it shouldn't:

  1. Stability: if the model re-learned from every payment, an outage would slowly become the new "normal" and stop alerting. That is the classic contamination problem.
  2. Scale and cost: summarising millions of payments into 48 rows per 5 minutes makes the maths cheap and fast.
  3. Statistics: a single payment says nothing; a 5-minute summary of hundreds of payments has a measurable noise level (Step 8).
  4. Privacy: summaries contain no card numbers or customer details (data minimisation).

In this demo the payments are simulated by lumio/world.py on top of real NAB demand data, and the dashboard's Play button replays them through exactly this flow at 1×–10× speed.

Step 1 — Data load¶

1.1 From one transaction to a 5-minute summary¶

What a collector sees is individual payments. Here we take one real segment-bucket from the dataset (Bank X · UPI · Android · North, Fri 7 Feb 10:00) and simulate every individual payment in it, then summarise them exactly as a collector does.

In [3]:
demo_csv = pd.read_csv(DATA / "payments_demo_10days.csv.gz", parse_dates=["ts"])
row = demo_csv[(demo_csv.ts == "2025-02-07 10:00") & (demo_csv.bank == "Bank X") & (demo_csv.channel == "UPI")
               & (demo_csv.platform == "Android") & (demo_csv.region == "North")].iloc[0]
g = np.random.default_rng(1)
n = int(row.volume)
median = row.p95_ms / math.exp(1.645 * world.LAT_SIGMA)                # payment times are log-normal
txns = pd.DataFrame({
    "txn_id": [f"T{100000 + i}" for i in range(n)],
    "time": [row.ts + timedelta(seconds=float(s)) for s in np.sort(g.uniform(0, 300, n))],
    "amount_$": np.round(np.exp(g.normal(np.log(row.avg_amount) - .08, .4, n)), 2),
    "latency_ms": np.round(g.lognormal(np.log(median), world.LAT_SIGMA, n), 1),
    "status": np.where(np.arange(n) < row.success_count, "success", "failed")})
txns["status"] = g.permutation(txns.status.values)
print(f"{n} individual payments in 5 minutes for one segment. First 6:")
display(txns.head(6))
summary = pd.DataFrame([{"source": "collector summary from these payments", "volume": len(txns), "success_count": int((txns.status == "success").sum()),
                         "p95_ms": round(np.percentile(txns.latency_ms, 95), 1), "avg_amount": round(txns["amount_$"].mean(), 2)},
                        {"source": "row actually in the dataset", "volume": int(row.volume), "success_count": int(row.success_count),
                         "p95_ms": row.p95_ms, "avg_amount": row.avg_amount}]).set_index("source")
display(summary)
say(f"**{n} transactions become 1 row.** Every 5 minutes, 48 such rows arrive (one per segment), about {int(demo_csv.groupby('ts').volume.sum().mean()):,} payments summarised per batch on average.")

1.3 Load into SQL — Lumio's real database schema¶

db.init_db() creates the same tables the live app uses (SQLite here; PostgreSQL in Docker). The 3-week history goes in as a bulk initial load (batch ETL); the live days will arrive later as 5-minute streaming batches (Step 10).

1.4 Streaming ingestion: how live batches arrive¶

In the app, the simulator (or a real collector) posts a JSON batch every 5 minutes to /api/ingest, which calls ingest.store(). Here we call the same function for the first three live batches.

In [9]:
demo_csv["app_version"] = demo_csv.app_version.map(lambda v: f"{v:.1f}")
svc_demo = pd.read_csv(DATA / "services_demo_10days.csv.gz", parse_dates=["ts"])
def batch(ts):
    py = lambda recs: [{**r, "ts": pd.Timestamp(r["ts"]).to_pydatetime()} for r in recs]
    m = py(demo_csv[demo_csv.ts == ts].to_dict("records"))
    s = py(svc_demo[svc_demo.ts == ts].to_dict("records"))
    return {"ts": ts.to_pydatetime(), "metrics": m, "services": s, "samples": []}
streamed = []
for ts in pd.date_range(config.LIVE_START, periods=3, freq="5min"):
    payload = batch(ts)
    out = ingest.store(payload)                       # ← the app's ingest function
    streamed.append({"batch time": ts, **{f"{k} stored": v for k, v in out.items()}})
display(pd.DataFrame(streamed))
print("Example of one JSON record as posted to /api/ingest:")
print(json.dumps(ingest.to_json(batch(pd.Timestamp(config.LIVE_START)))["metrics"][0], indent=1))

Step 2 — Cleaning¶

2.1 Structural validation (at ingest)¶

ingest.store() rejects records missing a required field. Validation at the door is structural only; judging whether the data is trustworthy is the quality gate's job.

In [10]:
bad = {"ts": "2025-02-07T00:15:00", "metrics": [
    {"ts": "2025-02-07T00:15:00", "bank": "Bank X", "channel": "UPI", "platform": "Android", "region": "North", "app_version": "5.1", "volume": 300, "success_count": 296, "p95_ms": 1800.0},
    {"ts": "2025-02-07T00:15:00", "bank": "Bank X", "channel": "UPI", "platform": "Android", "region": "South", "volume": 280}],   # missing fields
    "services": [], "samples": []}
print("Records sent: 2  →  stored:", ingest.store(bad)["metrics"], "(the incomplete record was rejected)")
with db.engine().begin() as c: c.exec_driver_sql("DELETE FROM metrics WHERE ts = '2025-02-07 00:15:00.000000'")
checks = pd.Series({"nulls": int(hist.isna().sum().sum()), "success_count > volume": int((hist.success_count > hist.volume).sum()),
                    "volume ≤ 0": int((hist.volume <= 0).sum()), "p95 ≤ 0": int((hist.p95_ms <= 0).sum()),
                    "exact duplicates": int(hist.duplicated(["ts"] + SEG + ["app_version"]).sum())}, name="rows failing check (history)")

2.2 The data-quality gate (quality.check)¶

Every 15-minute scan, before anything is scored, each segment's data is checked for completeness (did all three 5-minute buckets arrive?) and duplicates. Two real problems are planted in the live period. Let's run the app's gate on them.

In [11]:
def gate(window_start):
    ws = pd.Timestamp(window_start); we = ws + timedelta(minutes=15)
    raw = demo_csv[(demo_csv.ts >= ws) & (demo_csv.ts < we)].copy()
    clean, res = quality.check(raw, we.to_pydatetime(), [db.seg_key(*k) for k in raw.drop_duplicates(SEG)[SEG].values] +
                               [db.seg_key(b, c, p, r) for b in config.BANKS for c in config.CHANNELS for p in config.PLATFORMS for r in config.REGIONS])
    res = pd.DataFrame(res).T
    return raw, clean, res
for label, w in [("Normal window", "2025-02-07 09:00"), ("Collector stopped (Bank Z West)", "2025-02-07 14:00"), ("Duplicate records (Bank W North)", "2025-02-12 09:30")]:
    raw, clean, res = gate(w)
    print(f"\n{label}, {w}: {len(raw)} raw rows → {len(clean)} after de-duplication | status counts: {res.status.value_counts().to_dict()}")
    if (res.status != "ok").any(): display(res[res.status != "ok"][["completeness", "duplicates", "status", "note"]].head(6))
say("**Missing data is not a slowdown, and duplicated data is not a surge.** Held segments are not scored (no false page); duplicates are removed before scoring. In the app these decisions go to the `dq_checks` table and the *Data quality* tab.")

2.3 Aggregation to modelling windows (model.aggregate)¶

The model learns from 15-minute windows (the scan interval): 3 × 5-minute buckets per segment, with app-version rows combined.

A subtle point: you cannot average two p95 values. During a release, one segment reports two rows (v5.1 fast, v5.2 slow). The p95 of all payments together is the 95th percentile of the mixture of both groups, which mix_p95 solves numerically.

In [12]:
p95s, vols = np.array([[2124.0, 6878.0]]), np.array([[700.0, 300.0]])
naive_avg = (p95s * vols).sum() / vols.sum()
g2 = np.random.default_rng(0)
sim = np.concatenate([g2.lognormal(np.log(p / math.exp(1.645 * .35)), .35, int(v) * 1000) for p, v in zip(p95s[0], vols[0])])
display(pd.DataFrame({"method": ["volume-weighted average of p95s (wrong)", "mix_p95 (Lumio)", "check: simulate 1,000,000 payments and take the 95th percentile"],
                      "p95 ms": [round(naive_avg), round(float(mix_p95(p95s, vols)[0])), round(float(np.percentile(sim, 95)))]}).set_index("method"))

t0 = time.time()
W = aggregate(hist, config.SCAN_MIN)                 # ← the app's aggregation
W["seg"] = W.bank + "|" + W.channel + "|" + W.platform + "|" + W.region
print(f"{len(hist):,} 5-minute rows → {len(W):,} 15-minute windows ({W.seg.nunique()} segments × {W.ts.nunique()} windows) in {time.time()-t0:.1f}s")
display(W.head(3))

Step 3 — EDA for modelling¶

Three things the model must predict for every segment and moment: payment time (p95), success rate and volume. EDA tells us how to treat each one.

In [13]:

    "Success rate is bounded between 0 and 1 and modelled directly, weighted by volume.")

Both p95 and volume are right-skewed and multiplicative (a slowdown is '×2', not '+500 ms'), so Lumio models their logarithms. Success rate is bounded between 0 and 1 and modelled directly, weighted by volume.

Volume and payment time both follow hour of day, differ on weekends, and the payday Friday evening carries 1.7× the volume of a normal Friday evening. Channel and bank shift the whole level. These observations become the features in Step 4.

Step 4 — Feature engineering (model.features)¶

Feature Type Why
hour numeric, fractional (10:15 → 10.25) Time of day drives both demand and speed; fractional keeps 15-min resolution
dow 0–6 Weekly pattern
weekend 0/1 Weekend days behave differently (late nights, quiet mornings)
payday 0/1 15th / last day of the month, moved to Friday if on a weekend (world.is_payday)
payday_eve 0/1 Payday 16:30–22:30, when the rush happens
bank_i, channel_i, platform_i, region_i categorical codes Each segment has its own level; gradient boosting handles categories natively (no one-hot needed)

What is deliberately not a feature: anything measured now: current volume, error rate, upstream service time. The model's job is to say what should happen, using only things known in advance (the calendar and the segment). If it used the current error rate, it would "explain away" an outage as normal. This is a form of target leakage, and avoiding it is also why the app can pre-compute every expectation for the whole replay up front.

Step 5 — Train / validation / test split¶

Time-series data must be split by time: train on the past, test on the future.

Set Dates Used for
Train 17 Jan – 2 Feb 2025 (17 days, includes the 31 Jan payday) Fitting models
Validation 3 – 6 Feb 2025 (4 days) Comparing models and tuning hyperparameters
Test 7 – 16 Feb 2025, the live period, normal rows only Final, untouched evaluation of how well the model knows normal
(Production) All 3 weeks The final model is re-fitted on train + validation, as the app does

tr, va = (W.ts < "2025-02-03").values, (W.ts >= "2025-02-03").values
live_raw = demo_csv.copy()
LW = aggregate(live_raw, config.SCAN_MIN); LW["seg"] = LW.bank + "|" + LW.channel + "|" + LW.platform + "|" + LW.region
key = pd.read_csv(DATA / "answer_key.csv", parse_dates=["start", "end"]); key["scope"] = key.scope.apply(json.loads)
def in_scope(df, scope):
    m = np.ones(len(df), bool)
    for k, v in scope.items(): m &= (df[k] == v).values
    return m
LW["event"] = False; LW["y"] = 0; LW["context"] = "none"
for _, e in key.iterrows():
    m = in_scope(LW, e.scope) & ((LW.ts + pd.Timedelta("15min") > e.start - pd.Timedelta("30min")) & (LW.ts < e.end + pd.Timedelta("30min"))).values
    LW.loc[m, "event"] = True
    ctx = ("system-wide demand (storm)" if e.kind == "advisory" else "planned maintenance" if "maintenance" in e["name"].lower()
           else "payday rush" if "payday" in e["name"].lower() and e.kind == "not_incident" else e.kind)
    LW.loc[m & (LW.context == "none").values, "context"] = ctx
    if e.kind == "incident":
        LW.loc[in_scope(LW, e.scope) & ((LW.ts + pd.Timedelta("15min") > e.start) & (LW.ts < e.end)).values, "y"] = 1
te = ~LW.event.values
Xte = features(LW)

ax.set_yticks([]); ax.xaxis.set_major_formatter(mdates.DateFormatter("%d %b")); ax.set_title("Time-based split"); plt.show()

# Why not a random split? Leakage demonstration on the latency model
hgb_app = lambda: HistGradientBoostingRegressor(max_iter=350, learning_rate=.08, max_leaf_nodes=48, categorical_features=cat_mask, random_state=7)
Xa, Xb, ya, yb, wa, wb = train_test_split(X_all, ylat, w_lat, test_size=.2, random_state=0)
r_rand = r2_score(yb, hgb_app().fit(Xa, ya, sample_weight=wa).predict(Xb))
m_time = hgb_app().fit(X_all[tr], ylat[tr], sample_weight=w_lat[tr])
r_time = r2_score(np.log(LW.p95_ms[te]), m_time.predict(Xte[te]))
R["leak"] = (r_rand, r_time)
display(pd.DataFrame({"split": ["random 80/20 (shuffled)", "time-based (train past → test on the future live days)"], "R² (log p95)": [r_rand, r_time]}).set_index("split").round(3))
say(f"The random split reports R² = {r_rand:.3f}; the honest time-based test gives {r_time:.3f}. "
    + ("The random split looks better because neighbouring 15-minute windows of the same day end up on both sides, so the model is partly tested on days it has already seen. " if r_rand > r_time else
       "Here the gap is small, but the random split is still invalid in principle: it lets the model see the same days it is tested on. ")
    + "**Always split time-series data by time.**")

The random split reports R² = 0.829; the honest time-based test gives 0.808. The random split looks better because neighbouring 15-minute windows of the same day end up on both sides, so the model is partly tested on days it has already seen. Always split time-series data by time.

Step 6 — Model training & evaluation¶

Three candidate models for each target:

  1. Seasonal baseline: the average for that segment, hour and day type in the training data (what a good spreadsheet would do)
  2. Ridge linear regression: one-hot features, with hour as a category
  3. Gradient boosting (HistGradientBoosting): Lumio's production model, with the app's exact settings
In [18]:
def onehot(X):
    return pd.get_dummies(X.assign(hour=X.hour.astype(int).astype(str), dow=X.dow.astype(str),
                                   **{c: X[c].astype(str) for c in X.columns if c.endswith("_i")}), drop_first=True).astype(float)
OH_all = onehot(pd.concat([X_all, Xte])); OH_tr, OH_va, OH_te = OH_all.iloc[:len(X_all)][tr], OH_all.iloc[:len(X_all)][va], OH_all.iloc[len(X_all):][te]
def seasonal(y_train_df, df):
    k = ["seg", "hh", "wk"]
    t = y_train_df.assign(hh=y_train_df.ts.dt.hour, wk=(y_train_df.ts.dt.dayofweek >= 5).astype(int))
    prof = t.groupby(k).target.mean()
    d = df.assign(hh=df.ts.dt.hour, wk=(df.ts.dt.dayofweek >= 5).astype(int))
    return prof.reindex(pd.MultiIndex.from_frame(d[k])).values
targets = {"log p95 (payment time)": (ylat, np.log(LW.p95_ms), w_lat, {"max_iter": 350, "max_leaf_nodes": 48}),
           "success rate":           (ysuc, LW.success, w_suc, {"max_iter": 250, "max_leaf_nodes": 32}),
           "log volume":             (yvol, np.log(LW.volume.clip(lower=1)), None, {"max_iter": 300, "max_leaf_nodes": 48})}
rows, MODELS = [], {}
for tname, (y, y_live, wts, hp) in targets.items():
    preds = {}
    preds["Seasonal baseline"] = (seasonal(W[tr].assign(target=y[tr]), W[va]), seasonal(W[tr].assign(target=y[tr]), LW[te]), seasonal(W[tr].assign(target=y[tr]), W[tr]))
    rid = Ridge(alpha=1.0).fit(OH_tr, y[tr], sample_weight=None if wts is None else wts[tr])
    preds["Ridge regression"] = (rid.predict(OH_va), rid.predict(OH_te), rid.predict(OH_tr))
    gb = HistGradientBoostingRegressor(learning_rate=.08, categorical_features=cat_mask, random_state=7, **hp)
    gb.fit(X_all[tr], y[tr], sample_weight=None if wts is None else wts[tr])
    preds["Gradient boosting"] = (gb.predict(X_all[va]), gb.predict(Xte[te]), gb.predict(X_all[tr]))
    MODELS[tname] = gb
    for m, (pv, pt, ptr) in preds.items():
        ok_v, ok_t = ~np.isnan(pv), ~np.isnan(pt)
        rows.append({"target": tname, "model": m,
                     "train R²": r2_score(y[tr], np.nan_to_num(ptr, nan=float(np.nanmean(ptr)))),
                     "validation R²": r2_score(y[va][ok_v], pv[ok_v]), "validation MAE": mean_absolute_error(y[va][ok_v], pv[ok_v]),
                     "test R²": r2_score(y_live[te][ok_t], pt[ok_t]), "test MAE": mean_absolute_error(y_live[te][ok_t], pt[ok_t]),
                     "test RMSE": mean_squared_error(y_live[te][ok_t], pt[ok_t]) ** .5})
ev = pd.DataFrame(rows).set_index(["target", "model"]).round(4)
display(ev); R["eval"] = ev
floor = float(np.mean(np.sqrt(LW.success[te] * (1 - LW.success[te]) / LW.volume[te])))
R["succ_floor"] = floor
say(f"**Why is R² so low for success rate?** Success rate barely varies over time (about 98 % all day). What variation there is, is mostly **binomial sampling noise**: "
    f"with a few hundred payments per window, the success rate wobbles by ±{100*floor:.2f} points by pure chance, and no model can predict chance. "
    f"The model's MAE ({100*ev.loc[('success rate','Gradient boosting'),'test MAE']:.2f} points) is close to that noise floor, so it is doing as well as possible. "
    "**R² is the wrong yardstick for a nearly constant target**; what matters is that the expected level is right, so that a *drop* stands out (Step 8).")

Why is R² so low for success rate? Success rate barely varies over time (about 98 % all day). What variation there is, is mostly binomial sampling noise: with a few hundred payments per window, the success rate wobbles by ±0.73 points by pure chance, and no model can predict chance. The model's MAE (0.66 points) is close to that noise floor, so it is doing as well as possible. R² is the wrong yardstick for a nearly constant target; what matters is that the expected level is right, so that a drop stands out (Step 8).

Residuals are centred on zero with no pattern against the expected value, but their size depends on volume. That's why Lumio does not use one fixed error band: it scales each residual by a volume-based noise model (Step 8).

Step 7 — Hyperparameter tuning¶

Randomised search over the gradient-boosting settings, scored by time-series cross-validation on the training period (each fold trains on the past and validates on the next block). Then the best settings are checked on the validation week.

    m.fit(X_all[tr], ylat[tr], sample_weight=w_lat[tr])
    trs.append(mean_absolute_error(ylat[tr], m.predict(X_all[tr]))); vas.append(mean_absolute_error(ylat[va], m.predict(X_all[va])))
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(9, 3.4))
ax.plot(its, trs, "o-", color=TEAL, label="train error"); ax.plot(its, vas, "o-", color=AMBER, label="validation error")
ax.axvline(its[int(np.argmin(vas))], ls=":", color=INK); ax.set(xscale="log", title="Validation curve: number of boosting rounds (deliberately aggressive settings)", xlabel="max_iter", ylabel="MAE (log p95)"); ax.legend(); plt.show()
say(f"Train error keeps falling as the model gets more complex, while validation error bottoms out around **{its[int(np.argmin(vas))]} rounds**"
    + (" and then rises: that rise is **over-fitting**." if vas[-1] > min(vas) * 1.002 else " and then flattens.") + " This is how the number of rounds is chosen.")

Train error keeps falling as the model gets more complex, while validation error bottoms out around 50 rounds and then rises: that rise is over-fitting. This is how the number of rounds is chosen.

Step 8 — From prediction to anomaly score¶

A prediction alone does not raise an alarm. Lumio converts actual vs expected into a z-score: how many "normal spreads" away the segment is.

$$z_{\text{latency}} = \frac{\log(\text{actual p95}) - \log(\text{expected p95})}{\text{noise(volume)} \times \text{segment spread}}$$

  • noise(volume): sampling noise; fewer payments → larger noise (lat_noise, succ_noise, vol_noise)
  • segment spread: each segment's own extra variability, estimated robustly with the MAD (median absolute deviation × 1.4826), so past outliers don't inflate it

Now we train the model with the app's own Baseline().train(). It reads the training data from the notebook database with SQL, exactly as in production, and we check that it matches what we built by hand.

In [24]:
t0 = time.time()

manual = HistGradientBoostingRegressor(max_iter=350, learning_rate=.08, max_leaf_nodes=48, categorical_features=cat_mask, random_state=7).fit(X_all, ylat, sample_weight=w_lat)

nz = rr.groupby("bin", observed=True).agg(volume=("vol", "median"), spread=("res", lambda x: 1.4826 * np.median(np.abs(x - np.median(x)))))
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8.5, 3.4))
ax.plot(nz.volume, nz.spread, "o", color=TEAL, ms=7, label="observed robust spread of residuals")
vv = np.linspace(nz.volume.min(), nz.volume.max(), 100)
ax.plot(vv, lat_noise(vv) * np.median(list(base.seg_lat.values())), color=AMBER, lw=2, label="lat_noise(volume) × median segment spread")
ax.set(xscale="log", title="Fewer payments → noisier p95: the noise model follows the data", xlabel="payments in 15-min window (log)", ylabel="spread of log p95"); ax.legend(fontsize=8); plt.show()

Step 9 — Threshold tuning & detection metrics¶

The model gives z-scores; a threshold (the sensitivity slider in Settings → Alert rules) turns them into flags. The app's rules for each segment window:

  • latency flag: z_lat > sensitivity and ≥ 30 payments
  • success flag: z_succ < −sensitivity and ≥ 30 payments
  • volume flag: |z_vol| > volume_sensitivity and ≥ 20 expected payments
  • confirmation: flagged in 2 consecutive scans before it counts

Evaluated at the segment-window level against the answer key (label = inside a real incident's scope and time). Data-quality holds are applied first.

In [26]:
LW["buckets"] = live_raw.drop_duplicates(["ts"] + SEG + ["app_version"]).assign(win=lambda d: d.ts.dt.floor("15min")).groupby(["win"] + SEG).ts.nunique().reindex(pd.MultiIndex.from_frame(LW[["ts"] + SEG])).values
LW["hold"] = LW.buckets < 3
LW = LW.sort_values(["seg", "ts"]).reset_index(drop=True)
def flags(sens, vsens=None, confirm=2):
    vsens = vsens if vsens is not None else sens * config.DEFAULT_RULES["volume_sensitivity"] / config.DEFAULT_RULES["sensitivity"]
    enough = LW.volume >= 30
    f = ((enough & (LW.z_lat > sens)) | (enough & (LW.z_succ < -sens)) | ((LW.z_vol.abs() > vsens) & (LW.exp_vol >= 20))) & ~LW.hold
    if confirm == 2:
        prev = f.groupby(LW.seg).shift(1, fill_value=False)
        f = f & prev
    return f.astype(int)
inc = key[key.kind == "incident"]
days = LW.ts.dt.normalize().nunique()
def evaluate(fl):
    caught, ttd = 0, []
    for _, e in inc.iterrows():
        m = in_scope(LW, e.scope) & ((LW.ts + pd.Timedelta("15min") > e.start) & (LW.ts < e.end + pd.Timedelta("15min"))).values & (fl.values == 1)
        if m.any(): caught += 1; ttd.append((LW.ts[m].min() + pd.Timedelta("15min") - e.start).total_seconds() / 60)
    fp = ((fl == 1) & (LW.y == 0))
    handled = LW.context.isin(["system-wide demand (storm)", "planned maintenance"])      # later app layers: advisory + change calendar
    fp2 = fp & ~handled; tp = (fl == 1) & (LW.y == 1)
    return {"precision (model only)": precision_score(LW.y, fl, zero_division=0),
            "precision (+ context layers)": tp.sum() / max(1, tp.sum() + fp2.sum()), "recall": recall_score(LW.y, fl),
            "incidents caught": caught, "median min to detect": float(np.median(ttd)) if ttd else np.nan,
            "false-alarm scans / day (model only)": fp.groupby(LW.ts).any().sum() / days,
            "false-alarm scans / day (+ context layers)": fp2.groupby(LW.ts).any().sum() / days}
sweep = pd.DataFrame([{"sensitivity": s_, "confirm": c_, **evaluate(flags(s_, confirm=c_))} for c_ in [1, 2] for s_ in np.arange(2, 9.5, .5)])
d45 = sweep[(sweep.sensitivity == config.DEFAULT_RULES["sensitivity"])].set_index("confirm")
display(d45.round(3).rename(index={1: "1 scan (no confirmation)", 2: "2 scans (Lumio)"}))
R["d45"] = d45

**Where do the 'false alarms' come from?** The table answers it: almost all are **volume** flags during the **winter storm** (real NAB data: demand collapsed everywhere) and **latency** flags during **planned maintenance**. Outside known events there are **{none_fp}**. That's why the model is only one layer:
* the **system-wide demand advisory** turns the storm's hundreds of segment flags into one advisory to Business Operations, and
* the **change calendar** marks maintenance windows as expected.

With those two context layers, precision rises from **{d2['precision (model only)']:.2f}** to **{d2['precision (+ context layers)']:.3f}**. Grouping 48 segments into one story and the business guardrails complete the job, which is how the full app scores **19/19 with zero false alarms** (Proof tab).

* **Confirmation** (2 scans) costs about 15 minutes of detection time but halves the model-only false-alarm scans (compare the two rows above).
* **Choosing the sensitivity:** every incident is still caught up to a sensitivity of **{all_caught}**; above that, real incidents start to be missed. The default 4.5 keeps a safety margin for incidents milder than the planted ones. **Recall** at segment-window level is below 1 even when every incident is caught, because the first minutes and the less-affected segments inside a broad scope don't cross the line. The operational measure is the **incident catch rate**.""")

The operational measure is the incident catch rate.

Step 10 — Live scoring: rebuilding what the dashboard shows¶

Now we play part of the live period through the real pipeline: every 5 minutes a batch is ingested into metrics (ingest.store), scored against the model's expectations, and the scores are written to the bucket_scores table. That table is what the dashboard's main chart reads (/api/series). Every 15 minutes the window z-scores (window_scores) feed the heatmap and the detector.

We stream Friday 7 Feb, 08:00 → 23:55: the card-network outage (10:20) and the app v5.2 release (19:00).

In [29]:
RULES = config.DEFAULT_RULES
def score_bucket_rows(ts_from, ts_to):
    # same calculation as Detector.score_buckets()
    with db.engine().connect() as c:
        df = pd.read_sql(select(db.metrics).where((db.metrics.c.ts >= ts_from) & (db.metrics.c.ts < ts_to)), c)
    agg = aggregate(df, config.BUCKET_MIN)
    e_lat, e_succ, _, _, sd = base.predict(agg); e_vol, _ = base.predict_volume(agg)
    return [{"ts": r.ts.to_pydatetime(), "seg": f"{r.bank}|{r.channel}|{r.platform}|{r.region}", "volume": int(r.volume), "p95_ms": float(r.p95_ms),
             "success": float(r.success), "exp_p95_ms": float(e_lat[i]), "exp_success": float(e_succ[i]),
             "band_lo": float(e_lat[i] * math.exp(-3 * sd[i])), "band_hi": float(e_lat[i] * math.exp(3 * sd[i])), "status": "ok",
             "exp_volume": float(e_vol[i] / 3), "alert_hi": float(e_lat[i] * math.exp(RULES["sensitivity"] * sd[i] / math.sqrt(3)))}
            for i, r in enumerate(agg.itertuples())]

exp_before = base.predict(LW[(LW.seg == "Bank Y|Card|Android|North") & (LW.ts == "2025-02-07 10:30")])[0][0]
t0, n_batches, log_rows = time.time(), 0, []
with db.engine().begin() as c: c.exec_driver_sql("DELETE FROM metrics WHERE ts >= '2025-02-07'")      # restart the live stream cleanly
for ts in pd.date_range("2025-02-07 00:00", "2025-02-07 23:55", freq="5min"):
    out = ingest.store(batch(ts))                                         # 1. ingest
    if ts >= pd.Timestamp("2025-02-07 08:00"):
        rows = score_bucket_rows(ts.to_pydatetime(), (ts + pd.Timedelta("5min")).to_pydatetime())      # 2. score
        with db.engine().begin() as c: c.execute(insert(db.bucket_scores), rows)                       # 3. store for the dashboard
        if len(log_rows) < 4 or ts.strftime("%H:%M") in ("10:20", "10:25", "19:30"):
            log_rows.append({"batch": ts.strftime("%a %H:%M"), "rows ingested": out["metrics"], "rows scored": len(rows),
                             "max latency vs expected": f"{max(r['p95_ms'] / r['exp_p95_ms'] for r in rows):.2f}×"})
    n_batches += 1
display(pd.DataFrame(log_rows))
exp_after = base.predict(LW[(LW.seg == "Bank Y|Card|Android|North") & (LW.ts == "2025-02-07 10:30")])[0][0]
print(f"{n_batches} batches streamed in {time.time()-t0:.1f}s")
say(f"**The data changed; the model did not.** Expected p95 for Bank Y · Card · Android · North at 10:30, before streaming: {exp_before:.0f} ms; after streaming 288 batches: {exp_after:.0f} ms. "
    "New data is *compared with* the model, not *learned into* it. That's what keeps an outage from becoming the new normal.")

# The 15-minute scan: window z-scores for all 48 segments → the dashboard heatmap and the KPI strip
def scan_view(window_start):
    ws = pd.Timestamp(window_start)
    with db.engine().connect() as c:
        raw = pd.read_sql(select(db.metrics).where((db.metrics.c.ts >= ws.to_pydatetime()) & (db.metrics.c.ts < (ws + pd.Timedelta("15min")).to_pydatetime())), c)
    clean, dq = quality.check(raw, (ws + pd.Timedelta("15min")).to_pydatetime(), [db.seg_key(b, c_, p, r) for b in config.BANKS for c_ in config.CHANNELS for p in config.PLATFORMS for r in config.REGIONS])
    a = aggregate(clean, config.SCAN_MIN); a["ts"] = ws
    e_lat, e_succ, z_l, z_s, _ = base.predict(a)
    a["z"] = np.maximum(z_l, -z_s); a["seg"] = a.bank + "|" + a.channel + "|" + a.platform + "|" + a.region
    return a, dq
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(16, 4.4))
kpis = []
for ax_, w in zip(axes, ["2025-02-07 09:45", "2025-02-07 10:30", "2025-02-07 19:45"]):
    a, dq = scan_view(w)
    hm = a.assign(row=a.bank + " · " + a.channel, col=a.platform.str[0] + "·" + a.region.str[:1]).pivot_table(index="row", columns="col", values="z")
    sns.heatmap(hm.clip(-2, 12), cmap="YlOrRd", vmin=0, vmax=12, ax=ax_, cbar=ax_ is axes[-1], annot=hm.round(0), fmt=".0f", annot_kws={"fontsize": 7})
    ax_.set(title=f"Scan {pd.Timestamp(w):%H:%M}: z per segment", xlabel="platform · region", ylabel="")
    kpis.append({"scan": f"{pd.Timestamp(w):%a %H:%M}", "payments (15 min)": int(a.volume.sum()), "success %": round(100 * a.success_count.sum() / a.volume.sum(), 2),
                 "segments scored": len(a), "held by quality gate": sum(v["status"] == "hold" for v in dq.values()),
                 f"segments over sensitivity {RULES['sensitivity']}": int(((a.z > RULES["sensitivity"]) & (a.volume >= 30)).sum())})
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()
display(pd.DataFrame(kpis).set_index("scan"))

Step 11 — Monitoring & retraining¶

A model in production must be watched. Two questions: is it still accurate? and is the data still like the training data? (drift)

LWn = LW[~LW.event]
daily = LWn.assign(day=LWn.ts.dt.strftime("%a %d"), ape=100 * np.abs(LWn.p95_ms - LWn.exp_p95) / LWn.p95_ms).groupby("day", sort=False).agg(MAPE=("ape", "mean"), windows=("ape", "size"))
val_mape = 100 * np.mean(np.abs(W.p95_ms[va] - np.exp(base.lat.predict(X_all[va]))) / W.p95_ms[va])
# Drift: Population Stability Index of the volume distribution, each live day vs the training history
def psi(a, b, bins=10):
    q = np.quantile(a, np.linspace(0, 1, bins + 1)); q[0], q[-1] = -np.inf, np.inf
    pa, pb = np.histogram(a, q)[0] / len(a), np.histogram(b, q)[0] / len(b)
    pa, pb = np.clip(pa, 1e-4, None), np.clip(pb, 1e-4, None)
    return float(np.sum((pb - pa) * np.log(pb / pa)))
daily["volume PSI"] = [psi(np.log(W.volume), np.log(LW[LW.ts.dt.strftime("%a %d") == d].volume)) for d in daily.index]
fig, ax = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(15, 3.6))
ax[0].bar(daily.index, daily.MAPE, color=TEAL); ax[0].axhline(val_mape, color=AMBER, ls="--", label=f"validation MAPE {val_mape:.1f}%")
ax[0].set(title="Latency model accuracy per live day (normal windows)", ylabel="MAPE %"); ax[0].legend()
cols = [RED if v > .25 else AMBER if v > .1 else TEAL for v in daily["volume PSI"]]
ax[1].bar(daily.index, daily["volume PSI"], color=cols); ax[1].axhline(.1, color=AMBER, ls=":", lw=1); ax[1].axhline(.25, color=RED, ls=":", lw=1)
ax[1].set(title="Drift: volume PSI vs training (0.1 watch, 0.25 act)", ylabel="PSI")
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()
display(daily.round(3).T)
R["drift"] = daily
hi = daily.index[daily["volume PSI"] > .25].tolist()
say(f"Accuracy stays close to the validation level every day, so **no retraining is needed** during these ten days. The drift check flags **{' and '.join(hi)}** (PSI up to {daily['volume PSI'].max():.2f}): the winter storm. "
    "That is a **temporary** shift, not a new normal, so the right response is an *advisory*, not retraining. "
    "Retraining on storm days would teach the model that empty streets are normal.")

That is a temporary shift, not a new normal, so the right response is an advisory, not retraining. Retraining on storm days would teach the model that empty streets are normal.

Retraining policy (production recommendation)

Trigger Action
Scheduled: monthly Re-fit on a rolling 8–12 weeks of history, excluding windows inside confirmed incidents
Accuracy: daily MAPE above 1.5× validation for 5+ days Investigate, then retrain
Drift: PSI > 0.25 for 7+ days (a lasting change, e.g. a new bank onboarded) Retrain
Structural change: new segment, app, region Retrain (new categories)
Feedback: many "not useful" on one segment Adjust that segment's threshold first (the Learning tab); retrain only if it persists

Every new model is compared with the current one on the same validation week before it replaces it, the same champion / challenger idea as Steps 6–7.

Professor's likely questions on the pipeline¶

1. Does the model update with every transaction? No. Transactions are summarised into 5-minute rows; the model scores each new row against what it learned from history. It is re-trained on a schedule, not continuously, so outages never become "normal" (Step 0, Step 10).

2. Why aggregate to 5 / 15 minutes instead of scoring each payment? A single payment carries almost no signal; a few hundred have a measurable average, failure rate and p95 with known noise. Aggregation also scales to millions of payments and protects privacy.

3. How did you split the data, and why not randomly? By time: train 17 Jan – 2 Feb, validate 3 – 6 Feb, test on the 10 live days. A random split leaks neighbouring windows from the same day into training and overstates accuracy (Step 5).

4. What features did you engineer, and what did you leave out on purpose? Calendar (fractional hour, weekday, weekend, payday, payday evening) and segment identity. Anything measured "now" was left out, because it would leak the anomaly into the expectation (Step 4).

5. Why log-transform the targets? Payment time and volume are right-skewed and change multiplicatively; logs make residuals symmetric and comparable across segments (Step 3).

6. Why gradient boosting rather than linear regression? It captures interactions (e.g. Card × evening × payday) without hand-made terms, and it was best or equal on validation. Ridge and the seasonal baseline were kept as benchmarks (Step 6).

7. How did you tune it, and did tuning matter much? Randomised search with time-series CV, then checked on validation; the validation curve shows where over-fitting starts. The gain was modest: features and data quality mattered more (Step 7).

8. How do you avoid over-fitting? Time-based validation, the train vs validation gap, regularisation (min samples per leaf, L2), and a validation curve on boosting rounds.

9. Which evaluation metrics, and why not accuracy? MAE, RMSE, R², MAPE for the regression; precision, recall, F1, incidents caught and time to detect for detection. Incidents are rare, so accuracy would be misleading (Steps 6, 9).

10. How was the alert threshold chosen? A sweep of sensitivity against precision, recall, false alarms and incidents caught, plus 2-scan confirmation. The default keeps every incident caught with a safety margin; the false alarms that remain come from known contexts (storm, maintenance), which later layers handle (Step 9).

10b. Your model-only precision is low. Isn't that a weak model? No. The breakdown shows almost all of those flags are real volume collapses during the storm and real slowness during planned maintenance. The data really was abnormal, but it was not an incident. Separating "abnormal" from "actionable" is the job of the context layers, and with them precision is close to 1.

11. Why does a small segment get a wider band? Fewer payments mean more sampling noise. The z-score divides by a volume-based noise model times a robust (MAD) per-segment spread (Steps 3, 8).

12. What happens when data is missing or duplicated? The quality gate holds the segment (no scoring, a data ticket) or removes duplicates before scoring (Step 2).

13. How would you know when to retrain? Monitor daily error against the validation level and drift (PSI); retrain on schedule or on a lasting shift, never on a temporary event like the storm (Step 11).

14. Is the notebook really the same as the app? Yes. It imports the app's modules, trains with Baseline().train() from the same SQL table, and shows the predictions are identical (Step 8).
